Q: Mongo::Error::NoServerAvailable: No primary server is available in cluster A:

I was facing the same error from docker. This solution will be helpful who is using ruby on rails, mongodb and docker. Here is my config on docker-compose.yml

mongodb:
image: mongo:latest
container_name: mongodb
restart: always
ports:
  - "27017:27017"
environment:
  MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME: root
  MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD: password
volumes:
  - mongodb_data:/data/db

On the mongoid.yml file on the host section I was localhost:27017. But I should write docker service name mongodb.

development:
  clients:
    default:
      database: tutorials_development
      hosts:
        - mongodb

Q: Dynamic Array to stack blocks of calculations A:

This formula is ugly, but it does what you want in terms of printing the coordinates horizontally, admittedly by a decidedly brute-force approach:

=MAKEARRAY(6,2*COUNTA(Table1[Name]),LAMBDA(r,c,IF(AND(MOD(c,2)=1,r=1),"",IF(AND(MOD(c,2)=0,r=1),INDEX(Table1[Name],c/2),IF(AND(OR(r=2,r=3,r=6),MOD(c,2)=1),INDEX(Table1[Left],(c+1)/2),IF(AND(OR(r=4,r=5),MOD(c,2)=1),INDEX(Table1[Width],(c+1)/2)+INDEX(Table1[Left],(c+1)/2),IF(MOD(c,2)=0,IF(OR(r=2,r=6,r=5),INDEX(Table1[Top],c/2),INDEX(Table1[Top],c/2)+INDEX(Table1[Height],c/2)))))))))

I'm sure it could be done much more elegantly but this formula at least does what you want. I also tested by adding a third rectangle to your table and it correctly gave the coordinates of that.

(Obviously, replace "Table1" with your actual table name.)

The problem with your formula is that you calculate irow as INT((c-1)/2+1) , but then you use c (the column index of the array) in ifs c=1, and [if] c=2, . So basically you tell the formula what to do only for the first two columns. I think you meant to put irow in those two places. If so, that fixes your formula, but it still only works for two rectangles. The one above works for an indefinite number of rectangles.

Thus, your formula as a working version (again, only works for 2 rectangles without expanding the ifs block), would be:

=LAMBDA(tabular,
  LET(
    head,TAKE(tabular,1),
    body,DROP(tabular,1),
    iname,XMATCH("Name",head),
    ileft,XMATCH("Left",head),
    itop,XMATCH("Top",head),
    iwidth,XMATCH("Width",head),
    iheight,XMATCH("Height",head),
    nrows,ROWS(body),
    array,MAKEARRAY(6,nrows*2,
      LAMBDA(r,c,
        LET(
          irow,INT((c-1)/2+1),
          seq,MOD(r-1,6),
          IFS(
            irow=1,
            IFS(
              seq=0,IF(MOD(c,2)=0,INDEX(body,irow,iname),""),
              seq=1,INDEX(body,irow,ileft),
              seq=2,INDEX(body,irow,ileft),
              seq=3,INDEX(body,irow,ileft)+INDEX(body,irow,iwidth),
              seq=4,INDEX(body,irow,ileft)+INDEX(body,irow,iwidth),
              seq=5,INDEX(body,irow,ileft)
            ),
            irow=2,
            IFS(
              seq=0,IF(MOD(c,2)=0,INDEX(body,irow,iname),""),
              seq=1,INDEX(body,irow,itop),
              seq=2,INDEX(body,irow,itop)+INDEX(body,irow,iheight),
              seq=3,INDEX(body,irow,itop)+INDEX(body,irow,iheight),
              seq=4,INDEX(body,irow,itop),
              seq=5,INDEX(body,irow,itop)
            )
          )
        )
      )
    ),
    array
  )
)(Table1[#All])

Q: What makes the calling convention different? A:

In general, platforms define one or more calling conventions. There will generally be a default calling convention used by the platform's default C compiler. There will generally be a calling convention used by the platform libraries. These may, or may not, be the same.

In principle, a compiler can use it's own function calling convention for functions inside the program, and only use the "platform" defined convention(s) for calls that go outside the program.

In practice this is generally not considered practical for C/C++ compilers on Unix-like systems. On Unix-like systems the C standard library is generally considered part of the platform, not part of the compiler.

You can't fully solve this problem with annotations in headers for two reasons.

  1. IIRC under some circumstances it is legal to declare a standard library function without using the header.
  2. Many functions in the standard C library accept function pointers which can point at arbitrary user functions.

In theory, C++ allows use of different ABIs for regular functions and "extern C" functions, however in practice none of the major compilers do this and doing so would likely break a lot of existing code.

On non-unix systems you have a bit more flexibility. For example on Windows, the C standard library is usually supplied by the compiler vendor, and the Windows API uses explicit calling conventions (which on 32-bit systems are different from the default "C" calling convention), but doing so would still be likely to cause compatibility issues with external libraries..

Languages other than C and C++ generally have more flexibility.
